h: Why the lorries are local heroes
p: There's a good reason those vehicles take centre stage. Thornycroft built lorries and buses in Basingstoke for much of the twentieth century, and the town's big factory employed thousands of local people. Taskers, over in Andover, made traction engines and trailers. So when you're admiring a gleaming old wagon here, you're looking at something that was probably built just down the road, maybe by somebody's grandad.

Milestones opened in 2000 and is run by a charity that looks after museums across Hampshire. It's a museum that suits wet days and big families, and it works brilliantly with grandparents along, because they become the tour guides. Get them talking about the shops and kitchens and you'll hear stories you've never heard before.
Top tip: pace yourselves. It's easy to rush the first street and then flag by the time you reach the later sections, so plan a stop for a drink halfway round.

If you're staying in the area, Basingstoke has some surprising history close by. The ruins of Basing House in Old Basing were the scene of a famous siege in the Civil War. The National Trust's The Vyne, a Tudor house with lovely grounds, is just north of town. Jane Austen fans will want to know she was born at Steventon, a village a few miles away, and the Willis Museum in the Market Place has more on local life.
